content: A-Raf, also known as serine/threonine-protein kinase A-Raf, is an enzyme encoded by the ARAF gene in humans. It belongs to the Raf kinase family, which consists of serine/threonine-specific protein kinases. Compared to other members of this family, such as Raf-1 and B-Raf, relatively little is known about A-Raf. While it shares many properties with the other isoforms, its biological functions have not been as extensively studied. All three Raf proteins play a role in the MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase) signaling pathway. A-Raf differs from the other Raf kinases in several ways. It is the only Raf isoform regulated by steroid hormones. Additionally, the A-Raf protein contains amino acid substitutions in a negatively charged region upstream of the kinase domain, known as the N-region. These substitutions may contribute to its low basal activity. Like Raf-1 and B-Raf, A-Raf activates MEK proteins, which in turn activate ERK, ultimately promoting cell cycle progression and cell proliferation. In their inactive state, all three Raf proteins are located in the cytosol, bound to 14-3-3 proteins. Upon activation by Ras, they translocate to the plasma membrane. Among the Raf kinase family, A-Raf exhibits the lowest kinase activity toward MEK proteins. This suggests that A-Raf may have additional functions outside the MAPK pathway or may assist other Raf kinases in activating the MAPK pathway. Beyond phosphorylating MEK, A-Raf also inhibits MST2, a tumor suppressor and pro-apoptotic kinase that is not part of the MAPK pathway. By inhibiting MST2, A-Raf can prevent apoptosis. However, this inhibition is dependent on the splice factor heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein H (hnRNP H), which maintains the expression of full-length A-Raf protein. Tumor cells often overexpress hnRNP H. When hnRNP H is downregulated, the ARAF gene undergoes alternative splicing, preventing the expression of full-length A-Raf protein. Consequently, overexpression of hnRNP H in tumor cells leads to full-length A-Raf expression, which inhibits apoptosis and allows cancerous cells that should be destroyed to survive. A-Raf also interacts with pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), an isozyme of pyruvate kinase involved in the Warburg effect in cancer cells. A-Raf upregulates PKM2 activity by inducing a conformational change, shifting PKM2 from its low-activity dimeric form to its highly active tetrameric form. In cancer cells, the ratio of dimeric to tetrameric PKM2 determines the fate of glucose carbons. In the dimeric form, glucose is directed toward synthetic processes such as nucleic acid, amino acid, or phospholipid synthesis. In the presence of A-Raf, PKM2 is more likely to adopt the tetrameric form, leading to increased conversion of glucose carbons into pyruvate and lactate, thereby generating energy for the cell. This links A-Raf to the regulation of energy metabolism and cell transformation, both of which are critical in tumorigenesis. Additionally, researchers have proposed a model linking A-Raf to endocytosis. Upstream of A-Raf, receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) are activated, leading to Ras-mediated activation of Raf kinases, including A-Raf. Once activated, A-Raf binds to membranes enriched in phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PtdIns(4,5)P2) and signals endosomes. This process activates ARF6, a key regulator of endocytic trafficking. A-Raf has been shown to interact with several proteins, including EFEMP1, MAP2K2, PRPF6, RRAS, TIMM44, and TH1L.
